Program.cs @ stage-1: AddJwtBearer, TokenValidationParameters { ValidateIssuer = true, ValidIssuer = Jwt:Issuer, ValidateAudience = true, ValidAudience = Jwt:Audience, ValidateIssuerSigningKey = true, IssuerSigningKey = SymmetricSecurityKey(signingKey), ValidateLifetime = true }; no Events hook, no DbContext in validation. Issuer/Audience come from appsettings.json, so every copy of this API has them.

git grep -niE 'logout|revok|denylist|blacklist|AddSession|SignOut' stage-1 -- '*.cs' ':!*Migrations*' -> no hits. AuthController has only [HttpPost("login")].

RFC 6265 §4.1.1: "The semantics of the cookie-value are not defined by this document." ASP.NET Core cookie auth: "To create a cookie holding user information, construct a ClaimsPrincipal. The user information is serialized and stored in the cookie." (self-contained value in a cookie). RFC 9110 §11: credentials travel in header fields.

app-state.md: "The in-memory cache provider stores session data in the memory of the server where the app resides. In a server farm scenario: Use sticky sessions to tie each session to a specific app instance ... A better approach is to use a Redis, SQL Server, or Azure Postgres distributed cache". distributed.md: a distributed cache "Survives server restarts and app deployments." Round-1 overstatement fixed (both options now in claim and §4).

cookie.md (same self-contained model): "Once a cookie is created, the cookie is the single source of identity. If a user account is disabled ... The user remains signed into the app as long as the authentication cookie is valid." Remedy is a per-request check against stored data: "Validating the cookie on every request mitigates the risk of revoked users", via a LastChanged value in the user database. Stage-1 JwtBearer validation has no such check (claim 4).

app-state.md: "Session data is deleted either when the ISession.Clear implementation is called or when the session expires." and "If a cookie is received for an expired session, a new session is created that uses the same session cookie." (the old data is gone for the next request). Also follows from the lesson's definition of session (the record is the proof).

Conditional judgment, condition stated in the sentence ("When ending a login immediately matters more than avoiding a store"); follows from claims 9 and 10. identity-api-authorization.md frames the same trade-off: "a balance between immediate session invalidation and database performance". Not opinion-as-fact.

RFC 6750 §2.1 (WebFetch summary): clients sending an access token in the Authorization header "use the Bearer authentication scheme"; credentials = "Bearer" 1*SP b64token. §1.2: a bearer token is one "any party in possession of the token (a 'bearer') can use". RFC 9110 §11.1: an auth-scheme is a token "to identify the authentication scheme". Note: RFC 6750 is not itself a docs root; RFC 9110 (local) + 6750 on the same rfc-editor host agree.

issues.text: Unlisted claim: a specific status code and its cause after restart (502 = API still starting). True in the live run (502 at t+1..3s, 200 at t+4s; Caddy reverse_proxy to api:8080 while Kestrel is not listening), but it is not in the claims ledger.
issues.quote: If it prints `502`, the API is still starting — wait a few more seconds and run it again.
issues.fix: Keep the sentence. Add claim 13 to .meta.json: kind behavior, section 7, text 'Right after docker compose restart api, calls through Caddy (localhost:8080) return 502 until DonHang.Api is listening again; observed 502 for ~3 s then 200.', source_hint 'live: docker compose restart api + curl loop; Caddyfile handle /api/v1/* reverse_proxy api:8080', needs_verification true.

issues.text: Key a is again absolute. Replacing JWT_SIGNING_KEY in .env and recreating the api container makes the server reject this token (with every other token). What is true is that nothing can stop just this one token. Other options are clearly wrong, so the key stands, but it is overstated.
issues.quote: Support has no way to stop it today; it will be accepted until its eight-hour lifetime runs out, roughly seven hours away.
issues.fix: en: "Nothing in the app lets them stop just this one token; it will be accepted until its eight-hour lifetime runs out, roughly seven hours away." vi: "Không có gì trong app cho phép chặn riêng token này; nó sẽ còn được chấp nhận cho tới khi hết tám giờ sống, còn khoảng bảy giờ nữa."

issues.text: Overstated, same point as claim 6: rotating the signing key on the server does log this account out everywhere (along with everyone else). Claim 6 supports only 'no code'.
issues.quote: in an app like this one, where nothing on the server can do it.
issues.fix: Replace with: "in an app like this one, where no code on the server can do it."

issues.text: 'exactly the store' is too strong: a list of ended tokens only holds ended tokens, not a record per logged-in client like a session store. Claim 9 says only 'extra server-side state ... which the token model otherwise avoids'.
issues.quote: which is exactly the store tokens were avoiding.
issues.fix: Replace with: "which is the kind of store tokens were meant to avoid."

issues.text: The whole restart argument rests on the restarted API having 'the same signing key', but nothing says where the key lives. If the server holds it, I'd assume it sits in the process's memory like an in-memory session would, and is lost on restart too. I can't reconstruct why the key survives when a session wouldn't. Section 7's Suggested answer and quiz q5 (option a, explanations) depend on this step.
issues.quote: any copy of the API holding the same signing key can recognize the caller — and a restarted API recognizes the same token it issued before the restart.
issues.fix: Add one sentence after this one saying where the API gets its signing key at startup (e.g. 'The key is read from an environment variable when the API starts, so every copy and every restart gets the same one'), with a claim in .meta.json.
